transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I’m Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, Doctor. Well, I'm here because... it's my job, really. I'm a cleaner for some of the commercial buildings downtown. But lately, the thought of seeing a rat has gotten so bad that I just can't do parts of my job anymore. 

Which is a huge problem because my supervisor, Gary, is already breathing down my neck about my hours. Gary actually used to date my younger sister back in high school, which makes it so weird when he tries to act all authoritative with me now. My sister lives out in Ohio these days, actually. She just bought a house with this huge fenced-in yard for her dogs, she has three of them now, mostly beagle mixes, I think... 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, work. Yeah, I just can't go into the trash rooms or the basements of the older buildings anymore. I'll just freeze. Even when I tell myself it's probably fine and not really dangerous, you know? Just the idea that a rat might be in there is ruining everything.
Can you tell me more about your fear of rats? For example, is it just rats, or are there other animals or situations that bother you in a similar way?

Well, it's really just the rats. Mice don't bother me nearly as much, and spiders or whatever are fine. But rats... they just terrify me. I don't know why. I've tried to figure it out. I even watched this documentary on PBS a few weeks ago about the history of sanitation in cities. It was actually really fascinating. Did you know that back in the 1800s, they used to have people whose whole job was just to go into the sewers and look for lost coins and jewelry? They were called "toshers." Can you imagine? Wading through all that muck and... well, everything else down there. My uncle Pete used to work for the water department, actually, but he drove one of those big trucks with the vacuums on the back. He retired a couple of years ago and bought an RV. He and my aunt are driving around the country right now. Last I heard, they were somewhere in New Mexico. But yeah, anyway... I just don't have that kind of reaction to anything else. Just the rats.
How does the fear of rats specifically impact your daily life outside of work, if at all? And have you ever gone out of your way to avoid places or situations where you might encounter a rat?

Outside of work, I definitely avoid places. Like, I won't even take the trash out at my own apartment building if it's dark out. I just leave it by the door. But it's mostly the work routes that are the problem... I actively turn down any routes they give me if they have basements, storage rooms, laundry areas, or those alley dumpsters. I just refuse when I can. If Gary absolutely forces me to clean one of those spots, I have to keep the door propped wide open, and I just rush through it as fast as humanly possible. I feel completely scared and on edge the whole entire time, just waiting for something to scurry out. 

Speaking of laundry areas, though, the one in the basement of the Miller Building has these ancient Speed Queen washers. My grandmother used to have a Speed Queen! It was that ugly avocado green color, you know the one from the 70s? She had the matching refrigerator, too. She lived in this little house in upstate New York, and every summer we'd go visit and make homemade ice cream on the back porch. Peach ice cream, usually, because she had a peach tree right in the yard. The peaches were always so small, though, not like the giant ones you get at the grocery store now. I really wonder what they do to the fruit these days to make it so big. Probably all those chemicals they spray, don't you think? It can't be good for us... wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, avoiding places. Yeah, I just stay away from the dumpsters and basements if I can help it.
When you're in a place where you're afraid a rat might appear, do you notice any physical reactions like a racing heart, sweating, shaking, or feeling like you can't breathe?

Oh, absolutely. It's like... an instant reaction. If I'm down in one of those basements and I hear even just a tiny scratching sound near a wall, or if I see a shadow move by a pipe, my whole body just goes into overdrive right away. My heart starts pounding out of my chest, my hands get all shaky, and I just feel this overwhelming panic, like I have to get out of there before I can even think straight. 

It's actually a lot like how my dog, Buster, used to react during thunderstorms. He was a golden retriever mix, the sweetest boy, but the second he heard thunder, he would just shake uncontrollably and try to wedge himself under my bed. Which is funny, because he was way too big to fit under there, so he'd usually just get stuck halfway, and I'd have to coax him out with those little bacon-flavored treats. Have you seen how expensive dog treats are getting lately, by the way? I was at the pet store the other day just looking around—I don't have a dog right now, my apartment doesn't allow them, which is a real shame because they're such good company. The landlord, Mr. Henderson, is really strict about it. He even evicted a lady on the third floor last year because she was hiding a cat. I felt bad for her, but rules are rules, I guess. 

Anyway, yeah, the physical reaction is terrible. Pounding heart, shaking hands... it's just awful.
